title: Matching Integration Mechanism to Data Shape at a Claims-Adjustment Agent
description: Tests the ability to match retrieval strategy, integration protocol, tool scoping, and authorization to the actual shape and stakes of four distinct sub-tasks inside one agent, under a hard latency budget for part of the workflow.

scenario.background: A financial services company is building an internal agent for its claims-adjustment team. The agent needs to: (1) look up policy details from a structured claims database by policy number, (2) search a 40,000-document corpus of historical claim adjudication notes and internal guidelines, (3) call an external fraud-scoring API operated by a third-party vendor, and (4) hand off complex disputed claims to a specialized appeals agent that runs its own multi-step investigation workflow. The claims team has a 5-second latency budget for the initial triage response; appeals can run asynchronously over minutes.

characters.name: Elena Petrova
characters.concern: The 5-second triage SLA must hold even as the agent gains more capabilities.

characters.name: Marcus Webb
characters.concern: Each adjuster's agent session must only ever retrieve claims the adjuster is personally authorized to see.

questions.stem: Which retrieval/integration approach is correct for policy lookup (1) versus historical adjudication-notes search (2)?
options: Use RAG with vector search for both, since both involve retrieving claims-related information

Use a direct API/database call for the exact-match policy lookup, and RAG with hybrid dense+sparse retrieval, semantic chunking, and metadata filtering (claim category, date, region) for the unstructured notes search
Use RAG for the policy lookup and a direct database call for the historical notes, since notes are more structured than policy records
Skip retrieval entirely for both and rely on the model's training knowledge
questions.explanation: B is correct because policy lookup is a structured, exact-match query against a system of record — a direct API/database call is faster and more accurate than RAG for a deterministic lookup — while the historical notes are unstructured prose with natural-language queries, which is genuine RAG territory, and hybrid retrieval plus metadata filtering (so recent guidelines outrank a superseded one) matches how adjusters actually search. A misapplies RAG to a task that has one deterministic correct answer per policy number. C reverses the two data shapes. D discards both a system of record and a real retrieval corpus for no reason.

questions.stem: Which integration mechanism is correct for the external fraud-scoring API (3) versus the appeals-agent handoff (4)?
options: MCP for the fraud API (for future discoverability) and a direct tool call for the appeals handoff

A direct API integration for the fraud-scoring call (a fixed, single-purpose, well-known endpoint with no discovery or reuse benefit), and genuine agent-to-agent delegation for the appeals handoff (independent multi-step reasoning owned by a distinct capability domain)
Agent-to-agent delegation for both, since both involve calling an external capability
A single shared tool definition that handles both the fraud check and the appeals investigation
questions.explanation: B is correct because the fraud API is a fixed, single-vendor endpoint called the same way every time — there's no discovery benefit (the endpoint never changes) and no reuse benefit worth MCP's protocol overhead in a latency-sensitive triage path, so a direct integration is simpler and faster; the appeals handoff, by contrast, needs the appeals agent to plan, gather evidence, and reason over its own multi-step investigation independently, which is genuine agent-to-agent delegation, not a tool call. A over-engineers the fraud call. C misapplies agent-to-agent delegation to a simple, fixed API call. D conflates two capabilities with entirely different shapes and risk profiles into one tool.

questions.stem: Marcus requires that a junior adjuster's session never retrieve claims data the adjuster isn't personally authorized to see. What authorization design satisfies this?
options: A single shared service credential for the claims database and fraud API, since all adjusters are trusted employees

Authorize each request against the individual adjuster's own entitlements at the data/service layer, rather than a shared service credential, so a junior adjuster's session cannot retrieve claims above their authorized threshold
Rely on the system prompt to instruct the agent not to show unauthorized claims to junior adjusters
Restrict access by IP address of the office network only
questions.explanation: B is correct because authorization has to be enforced at the layer that actually controls data access, scoped to the individual adjuster's real entitlements — a shared service credential (A) means every adjuster's session inherits the same broad access regardless of their actual permission level, which is exactly the gap Marcus is worried about. C is a soft, prompt-level instruction that doesn't structurally prevent the retrieval. D authenticates a network location, not an individual's entitlements, and says nothing about which specific claims a given adjuster may see.

questions.stem: Given Elena's 5-second triage SLA, which configuration correctly matches latency budget to task depth across the triage path and the appeals workflow?
options: Run full reranking and extended thinking on the historical-notes retrieval during initial triage, and skip it entirely during the appeals investigation

Use a lighter, reranking-skipped hybrid-search configuration for historical-notes retrieval during the 5-second triage path, and reserve full reranking and extended thinking for the asynchronous appeals workflow, which isn't bound by the same latency budget
Apply the same retrieval configuration everywhere, since consistency matters more than latency
Remove the historical-notes retrieval from the triage path entirely to guarantee the 5-second SLA
questions.explanation: B is correct because the triage path's hard 5-second SLA means the more expensive reranking pass has to be skipped there in favor of a lighter hybrid-search-only configuration, while the appeals workflow — explicitly unconstrained by that budget — can afford the deeper reasoning and reranking that improves accuracy on a harder, asynchronous task. A inverts the actual constraint, applying the expensive step exactly where the latency budget can't absorb it. C ignores that the two paths have fundamentally different latency requirements. D discards a retrieval step the triage response actually needs, rather than right-sizing its depth to the available budget.

keyLearnings: Retrieval and integration mechanism should match the actual shape of the data: exact structured lookups get a direct API/database call, unstructured natural-language content gets RAG, fixed single-vendor endpoints get direct API integration, and independent multi-step delegation gets agent-to-agent handoff.
Authorization for agent tool calls must be scoped to the individual end-user's real entitlements at the data/service layer, never a single shared service credential.

A hard latency SLA on one path (synchronous triage) versus no SLA on another (asynchronous appeals) justifies using a lighter retrieval configuration on the constrained path and a deeper one on the unconstrained path.
Least-privilege tool scoping applies at the agent level too — a triage agent doesn't need visibility into how the appeals agent's internal tools work, only that it can delegate to it.
